title: Why One Drug Dose Doesn't Fit All
hook: The blood thinner warfarin can need up to a 20-fold different dose from person to person — and about half of that swing is written into two of your genes.
key_points: Warfarin has a narrow safe window: too little lets dangerous clots form, too much causes bleeding.
The dose people need to stay in that window varies up to 20-fold between individuals.
About half of that variation is genetic; the rest is age, diet, weight, and other drugs.
The two biggest genes are VKORC1 (warfarin's target) and CYP2C9 (which breaks the drug down).
Lower-activity versions of these genes mean a person needs a smaller dose to stay safe.
Matching dose to DNA — pharmacogenomics — is now written into warfarin's FDA label.
content_html: Give two people the same dose of the blood thinner warfarin and one might barely respond while the other bleeds dangerously. Warfarin is the classic case of pharmacogenomics — the idea that your genes help decide how a drug should be dosed.
extra_html: Warfarin works by blocking the recycling of vitamin K, which the body needs to make several blood-clotting proteins. The dose required to keep clotting in the safe zone varies up to twenty-fold from one person to the next. According to NCBI's Medical Genetics Summaries, roughly half of that variability comes from clinical factors like age, diet, and other medications — and much of the rest from genetics. Two genes dominate: VKORC1, the enzyme warfarin actually targets, and CYP2C9, which metabolizes the drug. Common low-activity variants in either gene mean a person resists or clears warfarin differently and usually needs a lower dose. Because getting it wrong is so dangerous, the FDA's warfarin label and clinical guidelines now spell out how genotype can guide the starting dose — one of the first places DNA-guided, personalized dosing entered everyday medicine.

related.title: How Genes Become Traits
related.hook: You inherit two copies of every gene — one from each parent — and the way those copies interact helps decide everything from eye color to blood type.

related.title: Mutations: When DNA Changes
related.hook: Every time a cell copies its DNA, tiny typos can slip in — most do nothing at all, a few cause disease, and rare ones fuel evolution.

flashcards.prompt: Why does the warfarin dose people need vary so much?
flashcards.back_html: The dose to stay in warfarin's narrow safe window varies up to 20-fold. Roughly half of that is genetic — mainly variants in VKORC1 and CYP2C9 — and half is clinical (age, diet, weight, other drugs).

flashcards.prompt: Which two genes most strongly influence how much warfarin a person needs?
flashcards.explanation_html: VKORC1 is the enzyme warfarin targets (vitamin K recycling); CYP2C9 breaks the drug down. Low-activity variants of either mean a lower dose is needed.
